jsonld.articleBody:
I’m excited to participate in the Digital Investment Facility Roundtable on Fostering Green Digital Infrastructure Investments in Africa hosted by the GIZ, tomorrow. 

Growing up in Nigeria, I witnessed firsthand the challenges and immense potential of digital access across the continent.

My goal is to help drive investments in sustainable, green digital infrastructure, so that more communities in Africa, especially those in underserved areas like the one where I grew up, can benefit from reliable and secure technology. This is key to unlocking opportunities in education, entrepreneurship, and economic growth.

Looking forward to engaging with key stakeholders, including Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH (
The European Commission, Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), and Ministries of Foreign Affairs from Finland, Estonia, Belgium, and France.

I’m honoured to join this conversation with investors, policymakers, and innovators dedicated to empowering Africa’s digital future in an environmentally responsible way.

Thank you to Bjorn-Soren Gigler, PhD, for sharing this opportunity.

#GreenTech #DigitalAfrica #Sustainability #Innovation #AfricaTech #DigitalInfrastructure #TechForGood

jsonld.headline: Had coffee with Abdelaziz Saidu this morning.
jsonld.articleBody:
Had coffee with Abdelaziz Saidu this morning. He’s the General Manager for Cisco across Nigeria and Ghana, and it was refreshing being able to catch up on what is happening in the West African tech/policy space. 

We covered a lot of topics: digital sovereignty, local data centres, compliance frameworks, and where Nigeria and Ghana are across the board. As you can imagine, the current realities are different from what the headlines report. 

I learn a lot every time I get to talk with Mr Saidu. I did not realise that, often, when someone sends money in Nigeria, the transaction record does not stay in Nigeria. Instead, it sits in the cloud, on a server that is usually abroad. These Nigerian companies and fintechs simply rent the space. The Central Bank of Nigeria, in a memorandum released in June, has instructed that this must change, on or before January 2027. 

This new policy is much harder to implement than it sounds. Most companies cannot pinpoint exactly where, who and what touches their data. The detail is lost in the verbiage and legalese of the contracts. This challenge is exciting for me because it is a core part of my work in Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) and security at Cyera, where we scan the data a company holds, classify its sensitivity, and show who can access it. 

Regarding the infrastructure, these companies need data centres to migrate their data to. The data centres must be built. They need power that stays on a 100% of the time. Someone must fund these requirements years before the people realise they need them. Rules can be written in a month, but the build-out takes money and time. 

In truth, a country of 200 million people should not keep its most important records in someone else's house. But the solution requires deeper thinking, planning and resourcing.

As always, grateful for the time and mentoring, Mr. Saidu. 

#africatech #fintech #nigeria #ghana #cybersecurity

jsonld.headline: Eight years ago, I was a 12-year-old intern learning about startups.
jsonld.articleBody:
Eight years ago, I was a 12-year-old intern learning about startups.

Today, I’m building one.

Excited to officially welcome Dayo Adebari  to the team at Splita.

Building a company is ultimately about the people you get to build with, and I’m excited about what we’re going to create together as we continue building the infrastructure behind seamless group payments.

A big thank you to Mr. Kola A. for connecting us.

When on a catch up call, he mentioned that someone in the UK was working on a similar problem around group payments, I was immediately curious. 

Dayo and I connected, started talking about the problem, and it quickly became clear we were thinking about many of the same challenges around payments infrastructure and how group transactions should actually work.

That introduction eventually led to Dayo joining us to lead engineer at Splita.

But my gratitude to Mr. Kola goes back much further than that.

In 2018, when I was just 12 years old, I had the opportunity to intern at Ventures Park, part of the Ventures Platform Fund ecosystem founded by Mr. Kola.

That experience introduced me to the world of startups for the first time.

During that internship, I worked with teams at Ventoven Limited, gaining early exposure to things like data security, cybersecurity, and server management, while also supporting several Africa-based startups with operational and administrative work.

More importantly, it was the first time I saw first-hand how technology and entrepreneurship were changing Africa.

Being in that environment, surrounded by founders, builders, and innovators, left a lasting impression on me. It showed me what was possible.

Years later, as we build Splita, it feels meaningful that the same ecosystem that introduced me to startups is now helping connect the people building the future together.

So thank you again Mr. Kola Aina, not only for connecting us with Dayo, but for continuing to mentor and inspire young Africans working to build and change the world.

You’ve truly built an ecosystem dedicated to catalyzing growth beyond capital.

#Splita #fintech #startups #buildinpublic #africantech

jsonld.headline: Spent the evening with Kola A.
jsonld.articleBody:
Spent the evening with Kola A. I interned for him in 2018 at Ventures Platform Fund, when I was about 13 years old, and eight years later he still picks up when I call and still asks the harder question instead of the polite one. 

He's also the reason I know Dayo Adebari, now my co-founder and CTO at Splita. We covered a lot: Splita and all our progress so far; how founders here in Nigeria are quietly folding AI into their operations; the datasets and data centers Africa still doesn't own; and the longer conversation underneath all of it about Nigeria and what technology can and can't fix on this continent. The bottleneck has never been talent or a lack of ideas. It's power, patient capital, and people willing to build for a decade instead of a cycle. Grateful for the time, Mr. Kola.

#africatech #venturecapital #startup #entrepreneurship

jsonld.headline: Just wrapped up Chainguard #Assemble2026 in NYC.
jsonld.articleBody:
Just wrapped up Chainguard #Assemble2026 in NYC. Still processing this one.

I walked into rooms with CISOs, engineers, and security leaders from companies like Cisco, Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, KKR, etc.

Grateful to the Chainguard team (especially Katie Kern) for creating space for me to be in those conversations.

What made this experience different wasn’t just the talks. It was seeing how seriously the industry is rethinking the foundation of software in the age of AI.

A few things that stuck with me:

1. AI is accelerating everything and expanding the attack surface: More code. More dependencies. More risk.
2. The shift is from writing code to trusting what’s running in production: This showed up everywhere, from CI/CD to agent workflows.
3. Secure-by-default is becoming the baseline: Not a feature, the foundation. 

You could see it in everything Chainguard announced.
AI agents are becoming a new class of dependency, and most teams are not yet ready for it.

The thing that surprised me most was that the conversations were not about moving faster; they were about moving fast without losing trust. That changed how I think about everything I am building right now.

Between working on authentication infrastructure and building Splita, the takeaway is simple:
You cannot bolt on trust later; it has to be built into the system.

I appreciate everyone who took the time to share insights and push my thinking. This is one of those rooms I know I will come back to.

Are we building systems we actually understand anymore?

Some great conversations by people building this future in real time:
Dan Lorenc (secure-by-default infrastructure + software supply chain)
Patrick Donahue (scaling trust across the SDLC)
Ram Ramani (why security has to start at the model level)
David Stern (limits of AI vs human judgment in security)
Dwayne McDaniel (software supply chain + secrets security)

Appreciate all the insights 🙏


#Chainguard #Assemble2026 #Cybersecurity #DevSecOps #SoftwareEngineering #AI #AISecurity #CloudSecurity #StartupLife #Fintech #Builders #Tech
Brandon Heard Brume Oduaran Razeen Alam Andrew Schwartz Josh H. Matt McCarrell Conor Quinlan Arun Sundarababu Trinity College-Hartford Career and Life Design Center Trinity College

jsonld.headline: What if we’re already too late?
jsonld.text: Why Nigeria Needs AI Policy For Its Universities — Before It’s Too Late
jsonld.articleBody:
What if we’re already too late?

While the world is busy building the next generation of AI talent, Nigeria is stuck asking the wrong questions: Should we be teaching AI? Instead, we should be asking: How do we lead?

My article, “Why Nigeria Needs an AI Policy for Its Universities — Before It’s Too Late,” has now been published in The Independent Newspapers Nigeria because I believe we’re standing at a turning point. The absence of a national AI policy in our universities isn’t just an oversight — it’s a threat to our future.

Young Nigerians are brilliant. But brilliance without infrastructure, guidance, and vision gets exported or extinguished. We’re watching other nations train innovators while we risk becoming permanent consumers in a world we should help build.

I outline a path forward — one that involves bold leadership from the Ministry of Education, the National Universities Commission, and Nigeria’s tech ecosystem.

AI isn’t just a technological shift. It’s a strategic one.

Read the full article here: https://lnkd.in/eM7b5MPG

Let’s stop playing catch-up.
Let’s start leading.

#AI #Nigeria #HigherEducation #NationalPolicy #Innovation #FutureReady
